newsitem.title: USA: Time CEO says not aware of Primestar deal.
newsitem.headline: Time CEO says not aware of Primestar deal.

text.p: Time Warner Inc chariman and chief executive Gerald Levin said Thursday he was unaware of any proposals that would merge Primestar, the satellite TV firm, with News Corp.
A planned merger between News Corp and EchoStar Corp unraveled and News Corp chairman Rubert Murdoch has been reportedly seeking another partner for a satellite service in the United States.
Time Warner is one of the partners in Primestar. Primestar is a satellite company controlled by TeleCommunications Inc, Time Warner, U S West, Comcast Corp and Cox Communications.
Levin spoke to reporters after the company's annual meeting at the Apollo Theatre here.
During the annual meeting, Levin said in a general presentation that "there are no major acquisitions to be made." Last October Time Warner acquired Turner Broadcasting.

Shareholders approved by a wide margin a proposal to annually elect directors, Levin announced at the meeting. But another shareholder proposal requiring the company's publishing operations to stop using chlorine-bleached paper was defeated by shareholders.
The Ancilla Domini Sisters, along with nine other organizations, had proposed a resolution. The groups argued that dioxins in the paper "probably cause cancer...and other health disorders."

After the meeting, Levin was asked by reporters if he would be opposed to the purchase of the Los Angeles Dodgers baseball team by News Corp's Fox Sports unit. Time Warner and News Corp have become arch rivals.
Levin said he would support whatever was "in the best interests of Major League Baseball." Time Warner acquired the Atlanta Braves baseball team when it bought Turner.

A shareholder, upset that the company's stock price was low, asked what Levin intended to do to lift shares. Levin said he expected the company's financial plans would lift the stock, adding shares have reached new highs in recent days.
In answer to another reporter's question, Levin was asked about the status of negotiations with U S West Media Group on restructuring their partnership.
Levin said the two sides continue to negotiate "to see if the partnership can be restructured," with talks currently focused on "values." He did not elaborate.

In an impassioned address from the auditorium floor, C. Delores Tucker, chairman of the National Political Congress of Black Women, took the company to task for distributing music by black 'gangsta' rap artist Lil' Kim.
Describing the lyrics as pornographic, Tucker accused the company of aiding in the corruption of American black youth. Tucker drew strong applause.
The group has been pushing to stop distribution of the controversial, sexually explicit music.
Levin said he was limiting his remarks due to related litigation but said the company seriously balanced artisitic freedom with social responsibility.
